# qualtdict

**License:** [MIT](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Project Status: Active - The project has reached a stable, usable state and is being actively developed.](https://www.repostatus.org/badges/latest/active.svg)](https://www.repostatus.org/#active)
[![Status at rOpenSci Software Peer Review](https://badges.ropensci.org/807_status.svg)](https://github.com/ropensci/software-review/issues/807)
[![check-standard](https://github.com/lyh970817/qualtdict/actions/workflows/check-standard.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/lyh970817/qualtdict/actions/workflows/check-standard.yaml)
[![test-coverage](https://github.com/lyh970817/qualtdict/actions/workflows/test-coverage.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/lyh970817/qualtdict/actions/workflows/test-coverage.yaml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/lyh970817/qualtdict/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/lyh970817/qualtdict?branch=main)
<!-- badges: end -->

[Qualtrics](https://www.qualtrics.com/) is widely used to collect
questionnaire and follow-up data, and the analyst's work begins when the
survey closes. Qualtrics describes a survey in a deeply nested JSON
structure: questions, choices, matrix items, loops, embedded fields and
scoring rules are spread across several API objects. The downloaded response
file refers back to them only through identifiers like `QID12_3_TEXT`, and
can contain hundreds of such columns covering question choices, matrix
items, text-entry fields, Loop and Merge iterations, embedded data, scoring
outputs and text-analysis sidecars. Before any analysis, every column has to
be matched back to the metadata, renamed, labelled with its response
options, and documented. Done by hand or in ad hoc scripts, that mapping is
slow, error-prone, and hard for anyone else to check, especially for surveys
with matrix, side-by-side or multi-select questions and repeated waves.

qualtdict makes that mapping explicit, readable and reproducible. From the
Qualtrics metadata it builds a Variable Dictionary: a flat table with one row
per exported response column, showing the question, item, response level and
label it belongs to, plus a generated variable name. The dictionary is easy
to inspect and validate, and it doubles as a codebook you can review with
collaborators or publish alongside the data.

Applying the dictionary to downloaded responses attaches that structure to
the data itself. Every column is renamed to its variable name; choice columns
carry their response options as value labels, and text and numeric columns
carry the question text as a variable label. You can tell what each column
is just by looking at it, so the response data are analysis-ready from the
first `glimpse()`.

[qualtRics](https://github.com/ropensci/qualtRics) handles the Qualtrics API;
qualtdict handles everything between the raw export and your analysis. It is
not a replacement downloader for qualtRics, and not a general survey-cleaning
framework.

## Installation

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("lyh970817/qualtdict")
```

qualtdict does not need Java. The `SystemRequirements` field of its
`DESCRIPTION` mentions Java only because the suggested openNLP package needs
it for POS-tag filtering, which the Semantic Names in qualtdict do not use.

## Credentials

`dict_generate()` and `survey_fetch_labelled()` read your survey from
Qualtrics, so they need Qualtrics API credentials. Your institution must
allow API access, and it must be enabled for your account; the person who
manages your Qualtrics account can give you your API token and base URL.
Store them once with `qualtrics_api_credentials()`, which qualtdict
re-exports from qualtRics:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(qualtdict)

qualtrics_api_credentials(
  api_key = "<YOUR-QUALTRICS_API_KEY>",
  base_url = "<YOUR-QUALTRICS_BASE_URL>",
  install = TRUE
)
```

The rest of the functions work on objects you already have and need no
credentials.

## A Variable Dictionary for your survey

Pass the survey ID to `dict_generate()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
survey_id <- "SV_XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX"

dict <- dict_generate(survey_id, variable_name = "question_name")
```

The rest of this README uses `glad_example`, a small example bundled with the
package: the metadata of a subset of the GLAD Study sign-up survey (four
demographic questions, the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 blocks, embedded data and scoring
variables) with synthetic responses. `glad_example$dictionary` is exactly
what `dict_generate()` returns for that survey.

```{r}
library(qualtdict)

dict <- glad_example$dictionary
dict
```

Every column of the dictionary, with its type:

```{r}
dplyr::glimpse(dict)
```

The columns that identify a row are:

- `response_column_id`: the column name in the downloaded Qualtrics response
  file, such as `QID1147_5_TEXT`. This is how the dictionary is matched to
  your data.
- `row_source`: what the column comes from: a survey `question`, an
  `embedded_data` field, a `scoring` variable, or a `text_analysis` sidecar.
- `qid`: the Qualtrics question the column belongs to. One question can
  produce many columns, such as one per matrix item or per ticked choice.
- `question_name`: the question name you set in the Qualtrics survey editor.
- `variable_name`: the name the column gets in your labelled data, unique and
  safe for export.

The other columns describe the content: the Survey Block, question text,
item text, response level and label, and the Qualtrics question type. A
column with response options takes one row per option. The first PHQ-9
item, "Little interest or pleasure in doing things", is one response column
with four levels:

```{r}
dict[
  dict$variable_name == "PHQ.DEP.1.0",
  c("response_column_id", "variable_name", "level", "label")
]
```

Embedded data fields and scoring variables appear alongside the questions:

```{r}
dict[
  dict$row_source != "question",
  c("response_column_id", "row_source", "variable_name", "question")
]
```

## Check the dictionary

`dict_validate()` reports Validation Findings: dictionary rows worth a second
look before you analyse the data.

```{r}
findings <- dict_validate(dict)$validation_findings
findings[, c(
  "severity", "response_column_id", "original_candidate", "variable_name",
  "reason"
)]
```

All findings here are suggestive: they report variable names that qualtdict
repaired. The items of the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 matrices and the choices of the
multi-select qualifications question share one Question Name, so their
names are numbered to keep them unique, and the hyphen in the scoring
variable names `PHQ-9` and `GAD-7` is not safe in an export variable name, so
they become `PHQ_9` and `GAD_7`.

A definite finding, such as two choices sharing one response code, would mean
the column cannot be labelled reliably. `dict_assert_valid()` raises an error
for such level-label findings, and `survey_fetch_labelled()` runs it before
downloading anything.

## Labelled survey data

`survey_fetch_labelled()` downloads the responses through qualtRics and
applies the dictionary:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
survey_dat <- survey_fetch_labelled(dict)
```

For the example survey, that call returns
`glad_example$labelled_survey_data`:

```{r}
survey_dat <- glad_example$labelled_survey_data
dim(survey_dat)
head(survey_dat[, c(
  "externalDataReference", "DEM.AGE.1.0", "DEM.SEX.1.0", "PHQ.DEP.1.0",
  "HEAD", "PHQRaw", "PHQ_9"
)])
```

Columns are named by `variable_name`. Choice columns carry their response
options as value labels, and text and numeric columns carry the question
text as a variable label:

```{r}
attr(survey_dat$PHQ.DEP.1.0, "labels")
attr(survey_dat$DEM.AGE.1.0, "label")
```

so tools that read labels, such as sjlabelled, can use them directly:

```{r}
table(sjlabelled::as_label(survey_dat$DEM.SEX.1.0))
```

`survey_export_findings()` lists dictionary columns that were missing from
the download. For the example there are none:

```{r}
survey_export_findings(survey_dat)
```

## One block at a time

`dict_split_blocks()` and `survey_split_blocks()` split the dictionary and the
data by Survey Block. Embedded data fields and scoring variables are not
assigned to a block by default, so they are kept under `"..unassigned"`.

```{r}
dict_blocks <- dict_split_blocks(dict)
names(dict_blocks)
unique(dict_blocks$GAD7[, c("response_column_id", "variable_name", "item")])

survey_blocks <- survey_split_blocks(survey_dat)
names(survey_blocks$GAD7)
```

## Semantic Names

If the Question Names in your survey are not good analysis names, ask for
Semantic Names, generated from the question text. Here `block_pattern` turns
each Survey Block name into a prefix:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
block_pattern <- function(block) {
  substring(block, 1, 3)
}

dict <- dict_generate(
  survey_id,
  variable_name = "semantic_name",
  block_pattern = block_pattern,
  block_sep = "."
)
```

Semantic Names are a readable convenience, not stable identifiers: they can
change with the survey text or the package version. They need the suggested
packages slowraker, SnowballC, stringi and tidyr.

## How To Cite

If `qualtdict` contributes to published work, please cite it. The citation
for the installed version is returned by `citation()`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
citation("qualtdict")
```
